Data: [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/), Palmer
Station Antarctica LTER, released under a
[CC0 licence](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). The dataset was
first published as an R package; I loaded it here with the
[palmerpenguins](https://pypi.org/project/palmerpenguins/) Python package
(version 0.1.6), a port of that original. 

This post is the same analysis as my R post, translated into Python with pandas and
matplotlib. 

Two of the penguins are missing their bill and body mass measurements, so they
do not appear in the figures below.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
```

```{python}
#| label: species-summary

peng_summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        count=("species", "size"),
        median_bill_length_mm=("bill_length_mm", "median"),
        median_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "median"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

peng_summary
```

```{python}
#| label: sort-data

peng_sorted = penguins.sort_values("bill_length_mm", ascending=False)

peng_sorted.head()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sorted
#| fig-cap: "Bill length against body mass, with species in the default alphabetical legend order."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

for species in sorted(peng_sorted["species"].unique()):
    subset = peng_sorted[peng_sorted["species"] == species]
    ax.scatter(subset["bill_length_mm"], subset["body_mass_g"], s=20, label=species)

ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)", fontsize=14)
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)", fontsize=14)
ax.grid(True, color="lightgrey")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.legend(title="species", fontsize=12)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: reorder-species

species_order = peng_summary.sort_values("median_body_mass_g")["species"].tolist()
species_order.reverse()

species_order
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-reordered
#| fig-cap: "The same data after reordering the species by median body mass, heaviest first, which changes the legend order and the colours."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

for species in species_order:
    subset = peng_sorted[peng_sorted["species"] == species]
    ax.scatter(subset["bill_length_mm"], subset["body_mass_g"], s=20, label=species)

ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)", fontsize=14)
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)", fontsize=14)
ax.grid(True, color="lightgrey")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.legend(title="species", fontsize=12)
plt.show()
```

## Findings

Using groupby and agg, I found the count and the median 'bill_length_mm' and
'body_mass_g' for each species. 'Gentoo' had the highest median body mass at 5000 g,
while 'Adelie' and 'Chinstrap' had the exact same median body mass of 3700 g.
'Chinstrap' had the longest median bill length at 49.55 mm, which is longer than
'Gentoo' even though 'Gentoo' is much heavier, so body mass and bill length do not
increase together across species. These are the same numbers I got in R, except that
pandas printed 49.55 mm where R printed 49.6 mm, because R rounded the value for
display.

Using the pandas sort_values function, I sorted the column 'bill_length_mm' in
descending order, but it had no effect on the figure. Python does not have factor
levels, so instead I made a list of the species ordered by median 'body_mass_g' and
reversed it, which is what fct_reorder and fct_rev did in R, and it gave the same
order of 'Gentoo', 'Chinstrap', 'Adelie'. I then looped through the species in that
order. This led to the figure changing, with 'Gentoo' being the first species in the
legend and having a blue plot colour now, and 'Adelie' changing from blue to green.
The data points on the plot remained the same, but the colour of the points changed.
This is because matplotlib assigns its colours in the order the species are plotted,
and we can see that changing the order impacts analysis and visualization.
